title: ECo-MoE: Embodiment-Conditioned Mixture of Experts
one_liner: Different robot body shapes activate different expert controllers automatically, letting evolution reuse and remix sensorimotor knowledge instead of learning everything from scratch.
lead: Robots come in endless shapes. You could train a separate brain for each shape (wasteful), or one universal brain for all shapes (too cautious and unrealistic). This paper splits the brain into modular expert controllers that the robot activates based on its own morphology. A small gating network reads the robot's shape (encoded as a list of numbers) and routes signals to whichever experts are useful, letting parts of control logic persist across body designs and new shapes borrow knowledge from ancestors.

paras: Robot design and control are tangled. A robot with six legs moves differently than a four-legged one, so each needs its own control strategy. Existing methods either train a separate brain for every robot shape (prohibitively expensive) or compress all shapes into a single monolithic brain that works for everything but never optimizes well for any one shape.

A naive beginner would train one brain per design, starting fresh each time. This wastes inherited knowledge: when evolution tweaks a robot's legs slightly, the new robot learns the same sensorimotor tricks all over again. Worse, it scales poorly—a realistic design space with millions of possible morphologies becomes untrainable.
The hidden problem: control knowledge is currently locked into one brain per morphology. When designs evolve, useful control patterns die with the old body design and must be rediscovered.

callout.html: Split the controller into expert modules and route signals to only the experts that match the current robot body shape.

steps.text: Robot morphology (bone structure, material, size) is represented as a list of numbers.
A simple neural layer scores how well each expert fits this specific body shape.
Convert scores to fractions between 0 and 1 that sum to 1 (softmax).
Blend each expert's sensorimotor commands by their routing weight.
Robots act, behavior is scored, body designs and expert mixture co-evolve.

paras: Instead of one monolithic brain per robot, the paper introduces a mixture of expert controllers. Each expert is a separate neural network that learns a sensorimotor strategy. The innovation is that these experts are not all used equally—a gating network decides which ones to activate based on the robot's decoded body shape.

hidden.h2: The compatibility of an expert to a body shape
hidden.name: Expert routing weight per morphology
paras: The hidden quantity is how much each expert's knowledge applies to each specific body design. When a robot shape is given to the gate, it outputs a weight for each expert (a number from 0 to 1, where 1 means use this expert fully and 0 means ignore it). This weight measures usefulness: an expert learned on four-legged movement gets high weight for four-legged designs and low weight for six-legged designs.

The paper measures this by training the gate (a simple linear layer plus softmax) jointly with the experts. As behavior improves through reinforcement learning, the gate learns to assign high weights to experts that reduce task error for each morphology, because the reinforcement learning algorithm nudges the gate weights toward whatever expert outputs reduce error—it learns which expert is actually useful. The paper also measures routing diversity—how spread-out the weights are—to avoid collapsing to a single expert.

heat.caption: Darker means expert is more useful to this body design. Borders mark which experts the gate selected.

reads.html: The gate learns to assign each expert a usefulness score. A score of 100% means use this expert; 0% means turn it off.

The embodiment-conditioned gate weights are computed as a learned linear layer over the morphology encoding (a list of numbers representing the genotype), applied to each expert through a softmax normalization.

mechanism.h2: Why modular routing beats monolithic brains
paras: Here is the causal chain. When a robot body shape evolves, the gate reads its morphology and routes control signals only to the experts that solve for that shape. Experts that learned useful tricks on ancestor designs stay alive in memory. A new four-legged variant does not restart from zero—it inherits four-leg experts from its parents and only adds tweaks. This speeds up learning because the expert modules encode reusable sensorimotor patterns: coordinating rigid segments, balancing on multiple limbs, sensing and reacting to ground contact.

A monolithic brain, by contrast, must balance all shapes at once, so it learns generic, overly conservative strategies that work everywhere but optimize nowhere. It cannot specialize. The modular approach enables specialization without duplication: each expert can be an extreme (very aggressive four-leg coordination, or ultra-flexible spinal movement) and the gate smoothly blends them based on the body it encounters, because specialization is cheaper—an expert that only handles four-leg movement can learn tighter, faster control than one that hedges for all shapes at once.

The paper also introduces evo-by-demo: a pretrained expert trained on a hand-designed blueprint is frozen into the mixture. The gate learns whether to use it. This acts as an anchor: evolution can now steer toward that pre-designed archetype because the gate automatically routes morphologies similar to the blueprint toward the pretrained expert, creating selection pressure on designs that match that shape.

stages.s: Robot morphology (body shape encoded as a list)
Gate network scores each expert's fit
Blend expert sensorimotor outputs by weight
Final control command for the robot

math.words: Gate weight for expert k equals softmax of a learned linear transformation of the morphology encoding, then blend each expert's output by its weight, then send the mixture to the robot.
math.equation: w_k(z) = softmax(W*z + b)_k;   action = sum_k w_k(z) * expert_k(state)
symbols: the routing weight assigned to expert k when morphology is z
the encoded morphology (latent vector, 512 numbers in the paper)
learned gate parameters (a small linear layer)
function that converts raw scores to weights; divides each score by the sum of all scores so weights add to 1
the control command from expert k given the robot's current state
the final blended control signal sent to the robot

math.note: The gate is a tiny learned layer that watches the morphology and decides which experts to trust; the softmax ensures the weights all fall between 0 and 1 and sum to 1.

charts.title: One brain per robot (baseline)
charts.note: Each design trains independently; no knowledge transfer; training cost scales with design count.

charts.title: ECo-MoE with pretrained experts
charts.note: New designs bootstrap from ancestral expertise; evolution discovers better morphologies faster because useful control patterns persist.

items.b: All morphologies route to the same expert.
items.html: If the gate ignores the morphology and always picks one expert, the framework collapses to a monolithic brain. The paper prevents this by adding a routing diversity penalty that pushes the gate to use all experts across the population.

If each expert is trained only on narrow designs, it fails on new shapes. The mixture framework mitigates this by forcing every expert to learn on every design (though with different weights), so each expert must capture broadly useful patterns.

items.b: Pretrained expert anchor fails to guide evolution.
items.html: If the pretrained expert is trained on a design too different from the evolved population, the gate may never trust it, and evo-by-demo provides no signal. Success requires the pretrained blueprint to be similar enough to the initial morphologies being evolved.

Train the gate and experts jointly under reinforcement learning. Use a diversity penalty to ensure experts are actually used. Start the initial morphologies near the pretrained archetype if using evo-by-demo.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple environment with a 2D locomotion task (e.g., moving a 3-segment body left or right, or a 2-leg vs. 4-leg hopper). Encode each morphology as a small latent vector. Train a mixture of 3-4 simple control experts (each a tiny neural network with 2-3 layers). Use a gate to route based on latent morphology. Evolve the latent coordinates across 20 generations. Compare: (1) per-robot learning (train a fresh brain for each evolved design), (2) one shared monolithic brain, and (3) ECo-MoE with gating. Measure average task performance and training time per design.
demo.metric_eq: average_performance = (sum of all robot fitness scores) / (number of designs); training_time = total wall-clock seconds; value_transfer = performance on new design before any retraining
demo.closing: ECo-MoE should show faster learning for new designs (high value transfer) and better average fitness than monolithic, because inherited expert modules jumpstart control instead of learning from zero.
